finding.claim: Authorization bypass on file deletion: `require_allowed` is an import alias of the boolean `is_allowed`, not the aborting `ensure_allowed`. Its return value is ignored, so the delete proceeds for any caller.
finding.source: Any request to DELETE /files/<fid>, including one with a missing or arbitrary user identity. The attacker only needs to know or guess a file id.
finding.sink: `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19, the file deletion.

trace.note: `from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed` aliases the boolean predicate under a name that implies enforcement
File loaded by URL id with no ownership check
`require_allowed(g.user, f, "delete")` returns False for unauthorized users, but nothing consumes the result (no if/abort)
`is_allowed` only returns a bool and never aborts

finding.guards_checked: acl.py `ensure_allowed` does abort(403), but delete_file does not use it. The rename route at views.py:26 does use it correctly. There is no other middleware auth. `before_request` only sets g.user and never rejects. Unknown fid raises KeyError (500), which is not a guard.

verdict.guard_found: require_allowed (alias of boolean is_allowed, views.py:4) is called at views.py:18 with its result discarded; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) would abort(403) but is only used in rename_file (views.py:26). before_request (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user.
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the bool-returning acl.py:4 is_allowed as require_allowed, views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement with no check, so `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19 runs for any caller, including anonymous ones.

finding.claim: Identity comes from a client-supplied HTTP header, `X-Session-User-Verified`, with no session, signature or token verification. Any caller can impersonate any user, including the owner of a resource, by setting the header. The 'Verified' name does not make it trustworthy unless a trusted proxy strips and sets it.
finding.source: Request header X-Session-User-Verified, set by any client that can reach the app directly.
finding.sink: `g.user` is used as the principal in `ensure_allowed` (views.py:26). Impersonating a grantee gives rename (write) access to that user's files. Combined with finding 1, no impersonation is needed for delete.

trace.note: `ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` checks grants keyed by that user string

finding.guards_checked: No authentication code, signature check or session lookup exists in the repo. Whether an upstream proxy strips or overwrites this header is not visible here, so exploitability depends on deployment. A direct-to-app or non-stripping proxy setup makes it exploitable.

verdict.guard_found: none in the repo. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 correctly, but it checks the unauthenticated g.user string. Any upstream proxy that strips the header is not visible here.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header, and views.py:26 passes it to ensure_allowed, which matches grants on that string (acl.py:5). An anonymous caller who knows a grantee's name can therefore get write access. Exploitability depends on whether a proxy strips the header, and that is not visible in the repo.
